entry: Extinct genus of saber-toothed felids. Smilodon lived in the [[Americas]] from the [[Pleistocene]] to the early [[Holocene]] epoch and was not closely related to the [[Tiger|tiger]] or to modern [[Cat|cats]]. Three species are recognized: *S. gracilis*, *S. fatalis* and *S. populator*. The largest, *S. populator*, from South America, weighed 220 to 470 kg. Smilodon hunted large herbivores such as bison and camels in North America. It died out in the end-Pleistocene extinction, around 13,000–9,000 years ago. The La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles hold the largest collection of its fossils.

Group of [[Museum|museums]], education and research centers created by the United States federal government. Founded on August 10, 1846, it operates as a [[Trust (law)|trust]] instrumentality and is not formally part of any of the three branches of government. It is named after its founding donor, British scientist James Smithson. Its historical holdings number over 157 million items, and it includes 21 museums, 21 libraries, 14 education and research centers and a [[Zoo|zoo]], mostly in [[Washington, D.C.]], with facilities also in [[Maryland]], New York and [[Virginia]]. More than 200 institutions in 47 states, [[Puerto Rico]] and [[Panama]] are affiliated with it. Almost all of its 30 million annual visitors are admitted free. Its annual budget is around $1.25 billion, about two-thirds from federal appropriations.

Process of discontinuing [[Tobacco smoking|tobacco smoking]]. Tobacco smoke contains [[Nicotine|nicotine]], which is addictive, and withdrawal symptoms often make quitting difficult. Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and a major risk factor for heart attacks, [[Stroke|strokes]], chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and [[Cancer|cancers]]. Quitting cuts the risk of heart attack by 50% after one year, and the risk of lung cancer by 50% after 10 years. Most smokers who try to quit do so without assistance, but only 3–6% of such attempts succeed long-term. Behavioral counseling and medications such as [[Bupropion|bupropion]] each raise success rates, and combining them works better than either alone. A 2018 [[Meta-analysis|meta-analysis]] of 61 [[Randomized controlled trial|randomized controlled trials]] found that about 20% of people using medication and behavioral help were nonsmokers a year later, compared with 12% who did not take medication. Many smokers in Canada and the United Kingdom have switched to [[Electronic cigarette|electronic cigarettes]].

Process of flavoring, browning, [[Cooking|cooking]] or preserving food, particularly meat, fish and tea, by exposing it to smoke from burning or smoldering material, most often wood. In Europe, [[Alder]] was the traditional smoking wood, but [[Oak]] is now more common. In North America, [[Hickory]] and [[Apple|apple]] woods are commonly used. Peat is burned to dry and smoke [[Barley|barley]] malt for [[Whisky|Scotch whisky]] and some beers. Heavy smoking was once combined with salt curing to preserve food, but modern transport reduced that need, and smoking became mainly a way to flavor food. The Torry Kiln, invented in 1939 in Scotland, is considered the prototype for modern large-scale smokers. Cold smoking, at 20–30 °C, flavors food without cooking it.

Illegal, often covert transport of goods, substances, people or intelligence across a border or in and out of facilities such as prisons, in violation of law. Motives include the [[Illegal drug trade|illegal drug trade]], illegal weapons trade, [[Human trafficking|human trafficking]], [[Prostitution|prostitution]] and [[Tax|tax]] evasion. Smuggling first became a recognized problem in England in the 13th century, after [[Edward I]] created a national customs collection system in 1275. Medieval smuggling focused on highly taxed exports, notably wool and hides. In 1724 [[Daniel Defoe]] wrote that smuggling was the reigning commerce of the English coast from the mouth of the Thames to Cornwall. Smuggling is also a common theme in literature, from Bizet's opera *Carmen* to the [[James Bond]] books and films, such as *Diamonds Are Forever* and *Goldfinger*.

Small portion of food generally eaten between meals. Snack foods are designed to be portable, quick and satisfying, and processed snacks are made to be durable and less perishable. They often contain sweeteners, preservatives and flavors such as chocolate or peanuts. Fruit, nuts, lunch meat and [[Candy|candy]] are also commonly eaten as snacks. In 2010, the average Canadian ate 300 snacks over the year. In the United States, peanuts arrived from South America via slave ships and became popular after the Civil War at baseball games and [[Vaudeville|vaudeville]] theaters. Pretzels, introduced by the Dutch in the 17th century, were rebranded to appeal to customers during Prohibition. In the [[Middle East]], nuts are a staple snack, and the most popular dip is [[Hummus|hummus]], a blend of [[Chickpea|chickpeas]], tahini, lemon and garlic.

Shelled [[Gastropod|gastropod]]. The name is most often applied to land snails, but also to many sea and freshwater species with coiled shells large enough to retract into. Marine snails make up most snail species. Most snails have a radula, a ribbon-like tongue with thousands of microscopic teeth, and many are [[Herbivore|herbivores]]. Snails live in habitats from deserts to the abyssal depths of the sea. Gastropods without a shell are called slugs. The largest living sea snail, *Syrinx aruanus*, has a shell up to 90 cm long.

Limbless reptile of the squamate suborder Serpentes. Snakes are ectothermic, air-breathing [[Vertebrate|vertebrates]] with elongated bodies covered in overlapping scales. Their skulls are more flexible than those of [[Lizard|lizards]], allowing them to swallow prey much larger than their heads. Snakes live on every continent except [[Antarctica]] and on most islands. Aquatic groups include the [[Sea snake|sea snakes]]. About 520 genera and more than 4,170 species are recognized in around thirty families, ranging from the 10.4 cm Barbados threadsnake to the [[Reticulated python|reticulated python]], up to 6.95 m long. Most species are non-venomous, and venomous species use [[Venom|venom]] mainly to kill prey. Snakes probably evolved from burrowing or aquatic lizards, perhaps during the [[Jurassic|Jurassic period]].

American multimedia [[Social media|social media]] and instant messaging app. Its pictures and messages, called Snaps, are typically accessible only briefly before recipients can no longer view them. Snap Inc. developed it, and it was first released as Picaboo on [[IOS|iOS]] on July 8, 2011. Its creators, [[Evan Spiegel]], Bobby Murphy and Reggie Brown, were former students at [[Stanford University]]. Stories show 24 hours of chronological content, and Discover carries ad-supported short-form content from brands. In 2023 Snapchat had over 300 million monthly active users, most of them aged 18 to 24.

Formula relating the angles of incidence and refraction of [[Light|light]] passing between two media. The ratio of the sines of these angles equals the ratio of the refractive indices of the two media. The law was first discovered by the Persian scientist Ibn Sahl at [[Baghdad]] in 984. [[Ptolemy]] had earlier found an inaccurate relation in [[Alexandria]]. Willebrord Snellius derived an equivalent form in 1621 without publishing it, and [[René Descartes|René Descartes]] published a derivation in 1637. [[Pierre de Fermat|Fermat]] derived it from his principle of least time.

Highly trained [[Military|military]] or paramilitary marksman. Snipers engage targets from concealment or at distances beyond the target's ability to detect them, using high-precision rifles with high-magnification optics. They often also serve as scouts or observers, feeding information back to their units. Military snipers are trained in stalking, [[Camouflage|camouflage]], tracking and target range estimation. Typical missions include shooting high-value targets, especially [[Officer (armed forces)|officers]], and providing feedback for [[Artillery|artillery]] and air strikes. The term became common in the [[World War I|First World War]]. It derives from the verb *to snipe*, meaning to shoot the game bird snipe, which arose in the 1770s among soldiers in British India.

Cue sport played on a rectangular table covered with baize, with six pockets. First played by British Army officers stationed in India in the second half of the 19th century, under the [[British Raj|British Raj]], it uses 22 balls: a white cue ball, 15 reds and six colored balls. Players pot balls in a defined sequence, and the player with the most points wins each frame. Army officer [[Neville Chamberlain]] devised early rules that combined [[Pool (cue sports)|black pool]] and pyramids. The standard rules were first established in 1919. Joe Davis won fifteen successive world championships between 1927 and 1946. The modern era began in 1969, when the [[BBC]] commissioned the television series *Pot Black*. Stephen Hendry and Ronnie O'Sullivan have each won the World Championship seven times.

American rapper, singer, record producer and actor. A key figure in West Coast [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]], he helped define G-funk and gangsta rap. He rose to prominence in 1992 with [[Dr. Dre]] on the album *The Chronic*. His debut album, *Doggystyle* (1993), debuted atop the Billboard 200 with 806,000 copies sold in its first week. Under the alias Snoop Lion, he released the [[Reggae|reggae]] album *Reincarnated* (2013). He has sold over 35 million records worldwide and co-headlined the Super Bowl LVI halftime show in 2022.

Beagle character in the comic strip [[Peanuts]] by [[Charles M. Schulz]]. He debuted in the strip on October 4, 1950, and his original drawings were inspired by Spike, one of Schulz's childhood dogs. Largely anthropomorphic and quick-witted, Snoopy spends his days atop his doghouse, pretending to be a [[World War I]] flying ace who fights the Red Baron, or writing stories on his typewriter. He is also known for his rivalry with Linus Van Pelt. Snoopy is widely considered the franchise's breakout character, and is more famous than Charlie Brown in some countries.

Icelandic historian, poet, knight and politician. He was twice elected lawspeaker of the Icelandic parliament, the Althing. He is commonly thought to have authored or compiled much of the *Prose Edda*, a major source on [[Norse mythology|Norse mythology]], and *Heimskringla*, a history of the Norse kings from legendary material to early medieval Scandinavian history. He is often taken to be the author of *Egil's Saga*. He was assassinated by men claiming to be agents of the king of [[Norway|Norway]].

Novel by the Japanese author [[Yasunari Kawabata]]. Considered a classic of [[Japanese literature|Japanese literature]], it was one of three novels cited when Kawabata received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1968. The story follows Shimamura, a rich, married [[Tokyo|Tokyo]] dilettante, who has a love affair with Komako, a provincial geisha, at a remote [[Hot spring|hot spring]] town. Komako falls in love with him, but his affection remains inconsistent. The novel ends with a fire in which a young woman falls from a warehouse balcony. Kawabata wrote it during Japanese militarism, and modern inventions such as the [[Train|train]] appear as part of the traditional setting.

headword: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
sort_key: snow white and the seven dwarfs
entry: 1937 American animated musical fantasy film produced by [[Walt Disney]]. Based on the 1812 German fairy tale "Snow White" by the [[Brothers Grimm]], *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs* was the first animated feature film produced in the United States and the first cel-animated feature. It premiered at the Carthay Circle Theatre in [[Los Angeles]] on December 21, 1937, and was released by RKO Radio Pictures. Despite initial doubts from the film industry, it earned more than $8 million internationally during its initial release, against a $1.5 million production cost, becoming the highest-grossing film of 1938. It was nominated for Best Musical Score at the [[Academy Awards]]. In 1989 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it as one of the inaugural 25 films for the National Film Registry. It is credited with ushering in the golden age of animation.

Felid species of the high mountains of Asia. Males are larger than females, and the snow leopard has thick whitish to grey fur with black rosettes, small rounded ears, broad paws and a thick tail, adaptations to cold, mountainous terrain. It lives at elevations of 3,000–4,500 m, from the [[Himalayas]] and the [[Tibetan Plateau]] to southern Siberia, [[Mongolia]] and western China. It is a solitary carnivore that mainly hunts [[Ungulate|ungulates]] and domestic [[Livestock|livestock]]. It forms a sister group with the [[Tiger|tiger]]. Listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, it is mainly threatened by poaching and habitat destruction.

Hypothesis that Earth's surface was nearly entirely frozen during one or more icehouse climates. It is most commonly associated with the Cryogenian Period, which had two major glacial episodes: the Sturtian, c. 717–660 million years ago, and the Marinoan, c. 650–635 million years ago. Proponents argue that it explains glacial deposits found at tropical latitudes. Opponents contest the geological evidence and the feasibility of a frozen ocean. Unresolved questions include whether Earth was fully frozen or a slushball with a thin band of open equatorial water. The episodes are proposed to predate the sudden radiation of multicellular life in the [[Cambrian explosion|Cambrian explosion]], and the most recent may have triggered the evolution of multicellularity.

Snow sport in which riders descend a slope standing on a single board with bindings securing both feet. Snowboarding was first developed in the United States in 1965, when engineer Sherm Poppen fastened two skis together for his daughters; the toy was called the snurfer. Tom Sims and Jake Burton Carpenter pioneered modern snowboarding, and Carpenter founded Burton Snowboards in 1977. Several riding styles have developed. The sport became popular worldwide in the late 20th century and has featured in the [[Winter Olympic Games|Winter Olympic Games]] since 1998 and the Winter Paralympic Games since 2018.

Salt of a fatty acid, used for cleaning and lubricating products. Toilet soaps are surfactants used for washing, usually made by saponifying fats or oils with an alkali such as [[Sodium hydroxide|sodium hydroxide]]. Their molecules form micelles that trap grease so it can be rinsed away, and soap kills microorganisms by disorganizing their membranes. In hard water, soap forms soap scum rather than lather. Metallic soaps thicken lubricating greases. Soap-like materials were produced in ancient [[Babylon|Babylon]] around 2800 BC. Sand or [[Pumice|pumice]] may be added to make a scouring soap that removes dead skin cells. Antibacterial soaps contain compounds such as triclosan, which has raised concern about antimicrobial resistance.

Long-running radio or television serial, frequently characterized by melodrama, ensemble casts and sentimentality. The term comes from radio dramas originally sponsored by soap manufacturers. Storylines run concurrently and intersect, and episodes typically end on a cliffhanger. BBC Radio's *The Archers*, first broadcast in 1950, is the world's longest-running soap opera. The longest-running television soap is [[Coronation Street]], first broadcast on ITV in 1960. In 1976 [[Time (magazine)|Time]] magazine called American daytime television "TV's richest market," as daytime serials earned profits several times their production costs.

Center-left political party in [[Germany]], founded in 1875 from a merger of socialist parties. It played a leading role in the German revolution of 1918–1919 and in founding the [[Weimar Republic]]. After [[World War I]] began in 1914, the party split between pro-war and anti-war members. After the rise of the [[Nazi Party]], it was the only party in the Reichstag to vote against the Enabling Act of 1933, and it was banned. Its 1959 Godesberg Program dropped its commitment to [[Marxism]]. It led the federal government from 1969 to 1982 under [[Willy Brandt]] and Helmut Schmidt. After losing the 2025 federal election, it became the junior partner in the Merz government. It sits with the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats in the [[European Parliament]].

Branch of anthropology that studies patterns of behavior in human societies and cultures. It is the dominant form of anthropology in the United Kingdom and much of Europe, where it is distinguished from [[Cultural anthropology|cultural anthropology]]. Social anthropologists isolate systems of social relations, such as kinship, economy, law, politics or [[Religion|religion]], and give priority to their organizational bases. Long-term [[Qualitative research|qualitative research]], including participant observation in intensive field studies, is traditionally favored over surveys. Anthropologists who studied [[Wall Street|Wall Street]], including Gillian Tett and Karen Ho, offered an alternative explanation for the [[2008 financial crisis|2008 financial crisis]].

Alteration of the social order of a society, including its institutions, behaviors or relations. Sustained at a larger scale, it may lead to social transformation. Social change does not necessarily imply social progress. It may describe a paradigmatic shift in socio-economic structure, such as the transition from [[Feudalism|feudalism]] to [[Capitalism|capitalism]], or social movements such as [[Women's suffrage|women's suffrage]] and the [[Civil rights movement|civil rights movement]]. Drivers include cultural, religious, economic, environmental, scientific and technological forces. [[Marxism|Marxism]] sees history as a struggle between social classes, while Thomas Kuhn argued that people keep using an apparently unworkable [[Paradigm|paradigm]] until a better one is commonly accepted.
